title: Value classes and what they compile to
goal: By the end you can write a validated value class, predict where it is a plain `long` and where it gets boxed, read its mangled names in `javap`, and give Java callers a safe way in.
opening:
At the print shop's parcel desk, every number on a job sheet carries a unit: 500 sheets, 2,500 grams. The clerk reads the units before a parcel goes out, and a sheet that says "weight: 500 sheets" goes straight back. In the back room the units are gone. The scale and the label printer only ever see numbers.

Code tends to lose its units much earlier. A `Long` called `grams` and a `Long` called `sheets` look the same to the compiler, so swap them in a call and it compiles. The classic fix is a small wrapper class, `Grams`, and it costs one object for every number. Kotlin's value class keeps the unit for the compiler and drops the object at run time. Mostly. The easy trap is to read "mostly" as "always".

In the last lesson, `inline` made the compiler paste away the object behind a lambda. This time it erases a wrapper. We'll see what a value class compiles to, find where the box comes back, read the strange names Java sees, and meet the one-field limit that waits for Valhalla. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: `@JvmInline value class Weight(val grams: Long)`. Which of these creates a `Weight` object on the heap (the memory where the JVM keeps objects) at run time?
options: `val total = a + b`, where `a` and `b` are `Weight`
`listOf(a, b)`
`class Parcel(val weight: Weight)`, when you build a `Parcel`
None of them: a value class is never boxed
warmup.why: A `List` holds objects, so each element is boxed into a real `Weight` (the compiler calls `Weight.box-impl(long)`). Inside `Parcel` the property is stored as a `long` field, and `a + b` compiles to a static method on two longs. The last option is the common belief, and the docs say the opposite: value classes are boxed whenever they are used as another type. The section on boxing lists every case.

sections.h: A value class is its own type to the compiler and a plain long at run time

sections.h: When the box comes back: generics, nullables, interfaces and collections
sections.body:
Value classes do get **boxed** after all. Boxing means wrapping the value in a real object on the heap, the way Java wraps a `long` in a `Long`. The rule fits in one line of the docs: inline classes are boxed whenever they are used as another type.

Back in the print shop, some shelves only take envelopes. The shared pigeonholes accept envelopes of any kind, but never a loose number. So a number on its way there goes into an envelope with its unit printed on the front, and comes out again when someone needs the number itself.

The demo uses a second value class, `Sheets`, which implements a small interface, `Counted`. Here are the four ways it can end up in an envelope:

```java
// Java's long and Long follow the same rule: a primitive where it can, a box when it must
static Object asGeneric(Object x) { return x; }

long sheets = 1_999;
Object boxed = asGeneric(sheets);     // autoboxed into a Long object
List<Long> list = List.of(sheets);    // another Long object
```

```kotlin
fun <T> asGeneric(x: T): Any? = x     // used as T: boxed
fun asNullable(s: Sheets?): Any? = s  // used as Sheets?: boxed
fun asInterface(c: Counted): Any = c  // used as Counted, an interface: boxed

class PrintRun(val sheets: Sheets)    // used as Sheets: stored as a long field
```

Four cases box. The first is a generic type parameter such as `T`. The second is a nullable type: `Sheets?` must be able to hold `null`, and a `long` can't. The third is an interface the class implements, and the fourth is anything typed `Any`, which includes every collection and `println`.

In the bytecode, each case shows up as a call to `Sheets.box-impl(long)` right before the call that needs the object. So a `List<Sheets>` holds one `Sheets` object per element. The docs draw the comparison you'd draw yourself: it's like `Int`, which is either a primitive `int` or a `java.lang.Integer`.

Equality still works by value. `s == Sheets(1_999)` compiles to `equals-impl0(long, long)`, a comparison of two longs. Identity doesn't exist. Identity asks "is this the very same object?", which is what Java's `==` asks of two objects and Kotlin's `===` asks too. For value classes, Kotlin refuses the question: `s === t` fails with `identity equality for arguments of types 'Sheets' and 'Sheets' is prohibited.`

That's stricter than Java, and for good reason. In Java, `Long a = 1_999L, b = 1_999L; a == b` is `false`, while the same code with `100L` is `true`, because the JDK keeps one shared box for each small number. That's a fine way to lose an afternoon.

Here the picture breaks a little. A real envelope stays the same envelope wherever it goes. A boxed value doesn't: put the same `Sheets` into two lists and you get two different boxes. That's one more reason Kotlin won't let you ask whether two of them are the same object.

**A value class is a plain value only while it's used as itself. Anywhere else, it travels in a box.**

In practice, a value class saves the allocation (the work of creating an object) wherever it's used as itself: fields, parameters, return values, arithmetic. That covers most of an app's own code. A busy loop that pushes millions of values through a `List<Sheets>` or a generic `Map` pays the same boxing as `List<Long>`. If that shows up when you measure, use a `LongArray`, as you would in Java.

Boxing stays invisible from Kotlin. Java, though, sees the bytecode exactly as it is, and the names in it look strange.

sections.h: Mangled names keep Java out, and @JvmName lets it back in
sections.body:
Look at that name again: `ship-P0HeBCA(long)`. The compiler adds a hash to the name of every function that takes a value class. The docs call this **mangling**, and it does two jobs.

The first job is to prevent clashes. A `JobId` value class wraps a `String`, so `describe(id: JobId)` and `describe(text: String)` would both be `describe(String)` in the bytecode. With mangling they become `describe-<hash>(String)` and `describe(String)`.

The second job is to keep Java away from functions that expect a checked value. A `-` can't appear in a Java method name, so `javac` can't call `ship-P0HeBCA`, however nicely you ask.

Mangling reaches further than functions. A class with a value-class property gets a private constructor, plus a public one with an extra `DefaultConstructorMarker` parameter that Java can't sensibly call. It also gets a mangled getter: the demo's `PrintRun` has `getSheets-auOsFv4()`. Members that return a value class are mangled too, so the lab's `Weight.Companion.parse` becomes `parse-D9kyZD4(String)`. A top-level function that only returns one is not: `parseWeight(String)` hands Java a plain `long`.

This is where the print shop picture breaks. Java comes in by the side door, and it can't read units at all. Either it can't call the function, or, once you open a door for it, it hands over a bare number that nobody checked.

For a single function, the quick door is `@JvmName`, which sets the name the function gets in the bytecode:

```java
System.out.println(ValueClassDemoKt.shipFromJava(199L));   // shipped 199 g
System.out.println(ValueClassDemoKt.shipFromJava(-5L));    // shipped -5 g: init never ran
// ValueClassDemoKt.ship(199L);                            // error: cannot find symbol
```

```kotlin
@JvmName("shipFromJava")
fun shipJava(weight: Grams): String = "shipped $weight"
```

Read the second Java line again. Java passes a raw `long`, and nothing runs `init` on the way in.

**@JvmName opens a door around your validation, so a function meant for Java must check its input again**, for example by building a fresh `Grams(weight.value)`.

Kotlin 2.2.0 added a fuller answer, `@JvmExposeBoxed`. It is still Experimental in Kotlin 2.4, which means it may still change, so you opt in with `@OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class)`. On a class, it adds a public constructor that runs `init`. On a function, it adds a version that takes and returns the box, `describeRun(Copies)`, next to the mangled `describeRun-D2JSnUo(long)`. The compiler flag `-Xjvm-expose-boxed` does the same for a whole module:

```java
Copies copies = new Copies(125);                     // a real constructor: init runs
System.out.println(ExposeBoxedDemoKt.describeRun(copies.doubled()));
```

```kotlin
@file:OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class)

@JvmExposeBoxed
@JvmInline
value class Copies(val count: Long) {
    init { require(count >= 0) { "negative copies: $count" } }
    fun doubled(): Copies = Copies(count * 2)
}

@JvmExposeBoxed
fun describeRun(copies: Copies): String = "a run of ${copies.count} copies"
```

Libraries see the same bytecode that Java does. Some find getters by name through reflection, that is, by inspecting a class's members while the program runs. A library that turns objects into JSON text, or one that saves them to a database, will meet `getSheets-auOsFv4`. Check how your libraries handle that before you put value classes into the classes they read.

Mangling, boxing and side doors all come from one fact: on today's JVM, a value class is a trick the compiler plays. That trick has a hard limit.

Without the opt-in, both annotations fail with `this declaration needs opt-in. Its usage must be marked with '@kotlin.ExperimentalStdlibApi' or '@OptIn(kotlin.ExperimentalStdlibApi::class)'`.

refs.title: Calling Kotlin from Java: inline value classes

sections.body:
Give a value class two properties and the compiler stops you: `value class must have exactly one primary constructor parameter.` So a paper size, `PaperSize(widthMm, heightMm)`, can't be a value class on the JVM in Kotlin 2.4. Neither can a weight that carries its own unit. There is no hidden flag for it either. Even the internal `-XXLanguage:+ValueClasses` earns only `warning: unknown language feature 'ValueClasses'`.

The limit comes from the JVM. Kotlin can erase a one-field class into its field because the JVM already has a `long` to erase it into. A value with two fields and no identity needs support from the JVM itself, and that is what Project Valhalla is building.

As the last track's Valhalla section said, JEP 401, Value Objects (Preview), was integrated into the JDK's main source tree on 31 July 2026. It ships in JDK 28, scheduled for March 2027, behind `--enable-preview`, the switch that turns on preview features. JDK 25, 26 and 27 don't have it.

Kotlin's design notes explain why `@JvmInline` is required today. It marks the current compile-time trick, so that a plain `value class` without the annotation can later compile to real Valhalla value classes. The notes call multi-field value classes before Valhalla "all theoretical", and no Kotlin release has a Valhalla mode yet.

For now, the one-field limit shapes your design. A paper size stays a data class, perhaps holding two value classes, a `Millimetres` for each side.

Where do value classes pay off? Anywhere two `String`s or two `Long`s could be swapped by accident: ids (`JobId`, `CustomerId`), counts and measures with one fixed unit (`Sheets`, `Grams`), and checked strings such as a postcode. Validation runs once, in `init`, and the type is the proof that it ran.

Where don't they? In functions that Java code calls a lot, unless you add `@JvmName` doors or `@JvmExposeBoxed`, and in classes that reflection-heavy libraries read. Keep value classes in your Kotlin code, and convert at the edges.

**A value class holds exactly one value. Anything with two parts stays a data class, for now.**

In the lab, you'll build two of them, a `Weight` and a `JobId`, and give Java a door that still checks.

try.title: Try a second field
steps: In `ValueClassDemo.kt`, change `value class Grams(val value: Long)` to `value class Grams(val value: Long, val unit: String)`. Run the demo.
Undo it. Which of your own types would you make a value class, and which would stay a data class?
try.expect: The build fails with `value class must have exactly one primary constructor parameter.` Single-value ideas such as ids, counts and measures in one fixed unit fit. Anything with two parts (a paper size with a width and a height, a weight with its unit) stays a data class for now.

compare.title: A job id: Java record vs Kotlin value class

java.title: JobId.java

kotlin.title: JobId.kt

compare.note: Both validate once, when the value is built, and both compare by value. The record is a real object: each `new` creates one, and a map keyed by job ids holds those objects. The value class is a `String` at run time wherever it is used as itself, so `findJob` costs exactly what a `String` parameter costs. The price is on the Java side: Java sees `findJob-<hash>(String)`, which it can't call, and it can't construct a `JobId` at all without `@JvmExposeBoxed`. JEP 401, a preview in JDK 28, adds `value record` to Java: a record without identity, which lets the JVM flatten it, that is, store its fields in place with no separate object.

worked.title: Make a swapped argument a compile error, then give Java a safe door

steps.say: The shop can reprint an old job for a customer. The reprint call takes two `String`s and a `Long`. Someone swapped the two ids in a quick fix, and it compiled.

static String reprint(String customerId, String jobId, long copies) { ... }

reprint(jobId, customerId, 200);   // swapped: compiles, reprints the wrong thing

reprint(jobId, customerId, 200)    // swapped: compiles, reprints the wrong thing

steps.say: Give each idea its own value class. The swapped call now fails to compile, twice, and nothing is allocated: in the bytecode the function still takes two `String`s and a `long`.

Check the Java view. `javap` shows `reprint-<hash>(String, String, long)`, so the older Java program that also reprints jobs can't call it any more. Don't reach for `@JvmName` here, because Java would pass raw values past every `init`. Add a Java entry point that takes the raw types and builds the value classes itself, so validation runs.
steps.alt_code:
// 3. the Java program calls the plain name; a negative count would fail inside Copies' init
String result = ReprintsKt.reprintFromJava("c-17", "job-2026-0042", 200L);

steps.say: Java can still swap the two strings in `reprintFromJava`, so the door is a compromise: it checks values, but it can't check names. That's why the type safety belongs in Kotlin, and the door belongs at the edge, used by as few callers as possible.

lab.title: Weight and JobId value classes with validation
steps: The shop's app weighs every parcel and gives every job an id. Run the tests. All nine fail.

In `Weight.kt`, add the `init` block (TODO 1), then write `plus`, `times`, `compareTo`, `toString` and `parse` (TODOs 2 to 5). `parse` reads kilograms, the way the shop's scale shows them, and keeps grams.
In `JobId.kt`, add the `init` block (TODO 6): 8 to 64 characters, ASCII letters, digits, `-` and `_` only.
In `Labels.kt`, write `parcelLabel`, then add the Java entry point (TODO 7) with `@JvmName`. Make it validate.
Run the tests until all nine pass. Then run `javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/main workbench.kotlin.l02.LabelsKt` and match each name to the Kotlin function it came from.
hints: `init { require(grams >= 0) { "weight must be non-negative, was $grams" } }` goes inside the class body.
`BigDecimal("1.2345").setScale(3)` throws `ArithmeticException: Rounding necessary`. That's what you want, so don't pass a rounding mode.
For ASCII only, test `it in 'a'..'z' || it in 'A'..'Z' || it in '0'..'9' || it == '-' || it == '_'`. `isLetterOrDigit()` alone also accepts letters such as `ö`.
TODO 7: `@JvmName("parcelLabelForJava") fun parcelLabelJava(weight: Weight): String = parcelLabel(Weight(weight.grams))`. Building a new `Weight` calls `constructor-impl`, which runs `init`.

Keep `override fun toString(): String` with its explicit return type. Kotlin 2.4.21 (and 2.3.21) crash with `Backend Internal error: Exception during IR lowering` when a value class's `toString()` infers its type from a Java call such as `toPlainString()` and the value is then used in a string template.
lab.done_when: All nine tests in `WeightTest` and `LabelsFromJavaTest` pass.

Write `@JvmInline value class Isbn(val value: String)` that rejects anything other than 13 digits starting with 978 or 979. Then write the Java record version. Which one allocates when you call `printCover(isbn: Isbn)` with it, and what is the JVM name of `printCover` in each language?

alt.title: Isbn.java

recap: `@JvmInline value class X(val v: T)` has one property, validates in `init`, is its own type in Kotlin, and is a plain `T` in the bytecode wherever it's used as itself.
It is boxed whenever it's used as another type: a generic `T`, a nullable `X?`, an interface, `Any`, and so every collection.
Functions that take a value class get mangled JVM names such as `ship-P0HeBCA(long)`. That avoids clashes between overloads and keeps Java out.
`@JvmName` lets Java call such a function, but Java passes the raw value and skips `init`, so validate again. `@JvmExposeBoxed` (Experimental, opt-in) gives Java a constructor that runs `init`.
A type alias is only a second name. A value class is a new type.
The limit: only one field on the JVM. Multi-field value classes wait for Valhalla, and JEP 401 is a preview in JDK 28.
closing:
We started at the parcel desk, where every number carries its unit until it reaches the machines. A value class is that unit: checked by the compiler, gone at run time, and back in an envelope whenever the value goes somewhere that only takes objects. Java comes in by the side door and sees bare numbers under strange names.

Now look in your own code for a function with two parameters of the same type side by side, two `String` ids or two `Long` counts. Each one is a swap that would compile.

Next, we'll let the compiler write a wrapper for us instead of erasing one. What does `by` forward, and to which object?

quiz.q: `@JvmInline value class Weight(val grams: Long)`. Which call boxes `w`?
options: `total(w, other)`, where `fun total(a: Weight, b: Weight) = a + b`
`log(w)`, where `fun log(x: Any?)`
`Parcel(weight = w)`, where `class Parcel(val weight: Weight)`
`w.grams * 2`
quiz.why: `Any?` is another type, so the compiler calls `Weight.box-impl` before `log`. `total` takes `Weight` as itself (two longs in the bytecode), `Parcel` stores a `long` field, and `w.grams` reads the long directly.

quiz.q: What can Java call for `fun reprint(id: JobId, copies: Copies): Boolean`, where both are value classes over `String` and `Long`?
options: `reprint(JobId, Copies)`
`reprint(String, long)`
Nothing: value classes can't be parameters of top-level functions
Nothing by that name: the JVM method is `reprint-<hash>(String, long)`, which javac can't call
quiz.why: Functions with value-class parameters are mangled, and the `-` makes the name impossible to write in Java. The parameters are the underlying types, so it isn't `reprint(JobId, Copies)` either. Add `@JvmName`, a raw-typed entry point, or `@JvmExposeBoxed` for Java.

quiz.q: Java calls `LabelsKt.parcelLabelForJava(-500L)`. In Kotlin: `@JvmName("parcelLabelForJava") fun parcelLabelJava(weight: Weight) = "Parcel $weight kg"`, and `Weight`'s `init` rejects negative weights. What happens?
options: It returns `"Parcel -0.500 kg"`: Java passed a raw long, so no `Weight` was constructed and `init` never ran
`IllegalArgumentException` from Weight's `init`
javac refuses the call, because the parameter is a `Weight`
`ClassCastException` at run time
quiz.why: `init` runs in `constructor-impl`, which only runs when someone writes `Weight(...)`. Java skipped that and handed the function a bare `long`. The fix is to build a fresh `Weight(weight.grams)` inside the Java entry point.

quiz.q: You try `@JvmInline value class PaperSize(val widthMm: Int, val heightMm: Int)`. What does Kotlin 2.4 do?
options: It compiles, and the JVM stores two ints in place
It compiles if you add `-XXLanguage:+ValueClasses`
It reports `value class must have exactly one primary constructor parameter.`
It compiles, but every use is boxed
quiz.why: On the JVM a value class has exactly one field. Even the internal flag `-XXLanguage:+ValueClasses` only earns `warning: unknown language feature 'ValueClasses'`, and the error stays. Multi-field value classes wait for Valhalla support in the JVM.

quiz.q: From the last lesson: `inline fun <T> printing(block: () -> T): T = queue.withPrinter(Callable { block() })`. What does the compiler ask for?
options: `noinline` on `block`
`crossinline` on `block`, because it's called inside the `Callable`
`reified` on `T`
Nothing: it compiles as written
quiz.why: `block` runs inside the `Callable`, another execution context, so a non-local `return` in the caller's lambda couldn't work. The compiler says `it might contain non-local returns` and asks for `crossinline`.

flashcards.front: What does `@JvmInline value class JobId(val value: String)` compile to where it's used as a `JobId`?
flashcards.back: A plain `String`. `JobId(...)` calls the static `constructor-impl`, which runs `init` and returns the same String.

flashcards.front: When is a value class boxed?
flashcards.back: Whenever it's used as another type: a generic `T`, a nullable `X?`, an interface it implements, or `Any` (collections, `println`).

flashcards.front: Why does `fun ship(weight: Grams)` compile to `ship-P0HeBCA(long)`?
flashcards.back: Mangling. It avoids clashes with overloads on the underlying type, and Java can't call a name with a `-` in it.

flashcards.front: What does `@JvmName` on a value-class function give Java, and what's the catch?
flashcards.back: A name Java can call. Java passes the raw underlying value, so `init` never runs: validate again inside.
An alias is another name, assignment-compatible with the original type. A value class is a new type: a `Long` won't go where `Grams` is expected.

flashcards.front: How many properties can a Kotlin value class have on the JVM?
flashcards.back: Exactly one: `value class must have exactly one primary constructor parameter.` More waits for Valhalla.

flashcards.front: What does `@JvmExposeBoxed` add, and what does it need?
flashcards.back: A public constructor that runs `init`, and boxed overloads Java can call. It's Experimental: `@OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class)`.

terms.plain: `@JvmInline value class X(val v: T)`: its own type in Kotlin, its single property `T` at run time where possible.
The type of a value class's one property, which is what the JVM actually sees.
Wrapping the underlying value in a real object of the value class, done when it is used as another type.
The hash suffix, as in `ship-P0HeBCA`, that the compiler adds to functions with value-class parameters.
Sets the JVM name of a function, which can remove the mangled suffix so Java can call it.
Experimental annotation (Kotlin 2.2+) that adds Java-callable boxed constructors and overloads.
A second name for an existing type. It adds no type safety.
The OpenJDK project that adds value objects without identity to the JVM. JEP 401 is a preview in JDK 28.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate who mostly writes Java asks why `fun ship(weight: Grams)` costs no allocation but `List<Grams>` does, and why their Java code can't call `ship`. Explain both in your own words.
explain_back.answer: A value class exists for the compiler, not for the JVM. Where the code uses a `Grams` as a `Grams` (a parameter, a field, a return value), the compiler passes the `long` inside it, so `ship` really takes a `long` and nothing is allocated. A `List` holds objects, so when a `Grams` goes into one, the compiler has to wrap the long in a real `Grams` object first, the same way Java wraps a `long` in a `Long`. That's boxing, and it happens whenever the value is used as another type: generic, nullable, interface or `Any`. Java can't call `ship` because the compiler mangles its name to something like `ship-P0HeBCA(long)`. The hash avoids clashes with a `ship(Long)` overload and keeps unchecked longs out. To let Java in, add a function with `@JvmName`, or one that takes a raw `Long` and builds the `Grams` itself, so the validation in `init` still runs.

deeper.body:
Two details that matter when you design with value classes.

A value class can wrap a generic type: `@JvmInline value class Box<T>(val value: T)`. The docs say the underlying type is then mapped to `Any?`, or to the upper bound of `T`, so at run time it's an `Object` field and you rarely save anything. Generic value classes help with type safety, not with speed.

The second detail is a compiler bug worth knowing about. In Kotlin 2.4.21 (and 2.3.21) this crashes the compiler with `Backend Internal error: Exception during IR lowering` and a `NoSuchElementException` from the string-concatenation lowering:

```text
@JvmInline value class W(val grams: Long) { override fun toString() = java.math.BigDecimal.valueOf(grams, 3).toPlainString() }
fun label(w: W) = "Parcel $w kg"
```

The trigger is the inferred return type: `toPlainString()` returns a Java platform type, `String!`, a type whose nullability Kotlin doesn't know. Write `override fun toString(): String = ...` and it compiles. It's a small, concrete argument for explicit return types on anything public: they keep platform types from leaking into your API, and here they also keep the compiler alive.

Finally, the history of the keyword, which explains old code you'll still meet. Kotlin 1.5.0 made these classes stable with the `value` modifier plus `@JvmInline` on the JVM, and deprecated the old `inline class` spelling with a warning. The design notes give the reason for the split: `@JvmInline` names today's erasure trick, which leaves the plain `value class` free to mean a real Valhalla value class one day.
